subsection: 7. The impact of EEC membership; case study: the impact of the EEC on fisheries

notes.b: Membership of the European Communities from 1 January 1973 opened the Irish economy to a common market and brought new financial transfers and rules.
points: Ireland accepted the common external tariff and the rules of the single market, which removed protection from many domestic industries.
Membership brought large transfers from the EEC budget, mainly through the Common Agricultural Policy and the regional and social funds.
The European Regional Development Fund was established in 1975, and Ireland, as a less prosperous member, received substantial funding from it (verify per-head comparison before quoting).
Membership gave Irish citizens rights to work and live in other member states, and it gave Irish representatives a seat in the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament.
The Common Agricultural Policy set guaranteed prices for farm products, which raised incomes for many Irish farmers, especially beef and dairy producers.
Irish farm output expanded in the 1970s, and agricultural exports to other EEC states grew rapidly.
Surpluses built up under the policy, and in 1984 the EEC introduced milk quotas that limited production on Irish dairy farms.
The benefits were uneven: larger farms gained most from price supports, while small farms in the west gained less.
Foreign firms set up factories in Ireland to gain access to the EEC market, and the IDA's grants and tax concessions were used to attract them.
Electronics, pharmaceuticals and chemicals were among the sectors that grew with foreign investment in the 1970s and 1980s.
Protected Irish industries, such as parts of the textile and footwear trades, declined as they faced competition from EEC producers.
Unemployment rose in the early 1980s as traditional industries contracted, showing that membership did not solve the economy's structural problems (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).

EEC directives on equal pay (1975) and equal treatment (1976) were incorporated into Irish law, supporting the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977 (see the notes on the status of women).
Membership exposed Irish people to European social and cultural trends, which affected attitudes to the Church and to the role of the state.
Irish sovereignty was affected in some areas, since EEC law took precedence over national law in matters covered by the treaties, and this was debated in the courts and in referendums.

notes.h: Case study: the Irish fishing industry before 1973
notes.b: The fishing industry was small, underdeveloped and largely based in coastal communities when Ireland joined the EEC.
points: Irish fishing was carried out mainly by small inshore boats, and much of the catch was sold fresh or salted for the domestic market.
Fishing was an important source of employment in coastal communities in the west and south-west, particularly in Donegal, Kerry and Cork.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara, the state fisheries board, was established in 1952 to develop the industry, with grants for boats and harbours.
The Irish fleet was small compared with those of France and Spain, and foreign trawlers fished much of the Irish shelf before 1973 (verify extent).

notes.h: Case study: the accession terms and the Common Fisheries Policy
points: On joining the EEC, Ireland secured a special arrangement giving its coastal waters priority access to Irish fishermen, with a zone reserved for the Irish fleet in the inshore area.
The Common Fisheries Policy was developed by the EEC in the 1970s and was agreed in its full form in 1983, opening Irish waters beyond the reserved zone to fleets of other member states.
The 1983 settlement introduced total allowable catches and national quotas for each species, which limited how much each state's fleet could land.
Irish negotiators argued that the quotas did not reflect the value of Irish waters, and the arrangements were a continuing point of conflict.

notes.h: Case study: development, ports and foreign fleets
points: Bord Iascaigh Mhara funded the modernisation of the Irish fleet, building larger vessels for deep-sea fishing and developing shore facilities.
Killybegs in Co. Donegal became Ireland's main whitefish port, with processing plants and a large fleet of purse-seiners and trawlers.
Castletownbere in Co. Cork developed as a major port for the pelagic and whitefish trades, and it served the south-west fishing fleet.
Foreign fleets, including Spanish and French vessels, fished in Irish waters under EEC rules, and disputes over access and enforcement were frequent in the late 1970s and 1980s.

notes.h: Case study: benefits and costs for coastal communities
points: Benefits: EEC funds and state grants helped build harbours, fish processing plants and larger boats, which created employment in some coastal towns.
Costs: quotas limited the catch, and small inshore fishermen often lost out to larger vessels with the capacity to fish more widely.
Fishermen and their representatives argued that Irish government negotiators gave away too much access, while the government argued that the policy had secured the best terms available.
Views also differed between regions: Killybegs and Castletownbere grew, while many smaller harbours declined as the fleet concentrated in fewer ports.

notes.h: Assessment: the gains and losses of membership
points: Achievements: membership brought secure markets for farm produce, large EEC transfers, and foreign investment in manufacturing.
Limits: unemployment rose in the early 1980s, and the benefits of the CAP and the fisheries policy were unevenly shared.
Contemporary view: supporters of membership argued that it was the only way to modernise an economy that had relied on protection and emigration.
Later view: historians note that membership supported growth and social change, but that the state's economic weakness in the 1980s showed the limits of relying on EEC transfers.

keyTerms.definition: A group of countries that trade without internal tariffs and apply a common external tariff to goods from outside the group.
The EEC system of guaranteed farm prices, support payments and market controls that shaped Irish farm incomes after 1973.
The EEC policy on access to fishing waters, total allowable catches and national quotas, agreed in its full form in 1983.
The Irish state fisheries board, established in 1952 to develop the fishing industry through grants and services.
The maximum tonnage of a species that may be landed in a year, set under the Common Fisheries Policy and divided between member states as quotas.
A limit on the amount of a product, such as milk or fish, that a country or producer is allowed to produce or land.
